facts.fact: Astrophysicist, teaching and outreach, compact binaries, SuperWASP Variable Stars, RAS Higher Education Award.
OU professor and planetary geochemist, light-element geochemistry, originator and PI of Beagle 2.
At the OU developed instruments for surfaces and atmospheres. PI for Huygens on Cassini.
He was a Director of ISSI from 2013 to 2016. Suggest “From 2013 to 2016 he was a Director of ISSI”.
British cosmochemist, emeritus professor at the OU, 40 years of oxygen-isotope work.
The official citation says “a French planetary scientist at the University of Bern”. His Scholar profile lists an OU post-doc. The rest matches the citation. Confirm his current affiliation with him.
OU senior research fellow, oxygen isotopes, wrote a popular meteorite book.
OU post-doc on achondrite differentiation and spectral analogues.
Discovered 14 November 1998 at Goodricke-Pigott by R. A. Tucker; named after Susan Jocelyn Bell Burnell (b. 1943), who discovered the first radio pulsar in 1967 with her thesis adviser Antony Hewish.

Bell Burnell's association with the Open University began in 1973 as a tutor; she was Professor of Physics at the OU from 1991 for ten years (to 2001), leading the physics department, then Dean of Science at Bath (2001-04).

Bell Burnell was President of the Royal Astronomical Society (2002-2004), the first female President of the Institute of Physics (October 2008 to October 2010) and the first female President of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (2014-2018). In August 2006 she presided over the IAU's adoption of the resolutions defining 'planet' and 'dwarf planet'. Her thesis adviser was Antony Hewish (spelt Antony).

JPL SBDB elements supplied by the user: a 2.365418760 au, e 0.109913567, i 7.982879°, node 97.395166°, peri 320.823874°, n 0.27092059°/day (period 1328.80 d, 3.638 yr), perihelion 2028-Apr-01.517 TDB (JD 2461863.0172). M0 at J2000 computed as n × (J2000 − tp) mod 360 = 84.64°.
Naming citation: NHM meteorite curator, carbon isotopes, meteorite recovery.
The citation dates from her NHM years. She returned to the OU in 2005, so the present tense is out of date. Suggest “formerly curator”.
Founded 23 April 1969, over 2 million part-time students, space exploration history.
Emeritus Professor at the OU, over 20 years observing minor planets and TNOs, starting with IRAS.
Japanese infrared all-sky survey satellite with widely used catalogues.
The OU was an international partner institute alongside Nagoya, Tokyo, ESA and other UK institutions.

The OU’s evidence to Parliament cites OU discoveries from Apollo and Luna samples. ESA survey of about 1,000 exoplanet atmospheres in visible and infrared.
UK lander deployed from Mars Express in 2003, found by MRO in January 2015 partly deployed. Aimed to detect carbon isotope signatures of life.

Conceived and led by an OU professor (Colin Pillinger). GAP used 12 ovens and stepped combustion mass spectrometry.
The Open University was the lead institute for Beagle 2's Environmental Sensor Suite (air temperature, pressure, wind, UV, dust), designed to monitor transient events such as dust devils.
Diamond-shaped, carbon-rich rubble-pile near-Earth asteroid.
Not yet. Orbit insertion is scheduled for 21 November 2026, and the two orbiters separate on 9 and 10 December 2026. Science starts in spring 2027. Suggest “arrives at Mercury in November 2026”.
Joint ESA–JAXA mission with two orbiters (MPO and Mio) studying the surface, composition and magnetic field. Launched 2018.
OU academics are on the M-CAM monitoring camera team analysing flyby images.
OU was a development partner, with instrument lead the University of Leicester, on MIXS.
Heavily cratered and inactive, rock and ice, possible ocean, farther from Jupiter’s radiation.
13 years at Saturn, Enceladus geysers, Titan’s surface, deliberate plunge in 2017 to protect the moons.
Documented OU Cassini work is on the Cosmic Dust Analyser (calibration and dust composition) and Huygens SSP. Ring and magnetosphere leadership not found.
Proposed Canadian-led UV and blue-optical space telescope with a field far wider than Hubble’s, for cosmology and galaxy formation.
CEI awarded £2.1 million for testing and space qualification of UV detectors for CASTOR, a Canadian-led 1 m telescope targeting about 2030.
CIS303 and CIS120 detectors from Teledyne e2v. Electro-optical testing, space qualification, and comparison of UV coatings and enhancement.
India’s first lunar probe. International instruments, 3D mapping and mineralogy, evidence of water molecules, operated about ten months.
CEI proton radiation assessment of C1XS’s 24 CCD54 detectors using SPENVIS. 14 modules characterised and ten recommended. Continuing advisory role.

Listed on the CEI mission page and the OU space research page. Follows directly from the Chandrayaan-1 entry. type: mission; parent: Moon; status: Operational (orbiter); launch_year: 2019; orbit: lunar polar orbit, about 100 km; description: India’s second lunar mission. Its orbiter has mapped the Moon since 2019. The Vikram lander was lost during landing.; ou_involvement: The Centre for Electronic Imaging characterised the CCD236 swept-charge devices for the CLASS X-ray spectrometer, which maps the Moon’s elements. It analysed radiation damage, showed a factor-of-two gain in radiation hardness, and produced the instrument’s quantum-efficiency calibration. CLASS uses 16 CCD236s.
Returned about 2 kg (1,731 g) in December 2020 from young mare basalts in Oceanus Procellarum. Automated docking in lunar orbit.
Actual site (Statio Tianchuan) is 43.06° N, 51.92° W, so lon should be about −51.9. The current value is about 200 km off.
CNSA named seven institutions from six countries on 24 April 2025, and the OU was one. Mahesh Anand then collected 60 mg in China. “Loan beginning in April 2025” should read “awarded in April 2025”.
Jupiter-family comet, two-lobed “rubber duck”, low density, dust and ices, jets near the Sun.
ESA mission that waits at L2 for a pristine comet, then flies by.
The OU light-gas gun fires particles at several km/s to test DISC’s dust shield.
First comet with dust sampled and returned. Rugged nucleus with steep-walled depressions.
DART struck Dimorphos on 26 September 2022; Didymos's closest approach to Earth was 4 October 2022 at about 0.071 AU.
Dimorphos is about 150–160 m across; DART shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes.
Didymos model extent 818 × 802 × 605 m (flattened at the poles, a spinning-top shape); DRACO imaging of Didymos was limited to about 3.7 m resolution; Didymos pole RA 66.83°, Dec −73.0° (ICRF).
Shape models: Didymos v003 and Dimorphos v004 from DART DRACO and LICIACube LUKE images (body-fixed, km, +Z = north pole). Used: Didymos 4.657 m and Dimorphos 0.972 m global OBJs.
JPL SBDB (epoch JD 2461200.5): a 1.64271 AU, e 0.38312, i 3.414°, node 72.986°, peri 319.581°, mean motion 0.46813°/day; perihelion 1.013 AU, aphelion 2.272 AU. Diameter 0.78 km, rotation 2.2593 h.
Dimorphos model extent 178 × 169 × 115 m. Its rotation after the DART impact is under study (possible non-synchronous or tumbling state), which Hera will measure.

Post-impact orbit of Dimorphos: period 11.3674 ± 0.0004 h (after settling from 11.377 h), eccentricity 0.0274 ± 0.0015; Didymos pole ecliptic latitude −80.7 ± 0.5° (so the orbit is retrograde, inclined about 170.7° to the ecliptic).
Post-impact semi-major axis 1.144 ± 0.070 km; period 11 h 22 m 03 s.
Only known planet with life, N₂–O₂ atmosphere, plate tectonics, liquid water in the habitable zone.
No OU publication or project found for machine learning on satellite imagery (deforestation, urban growth, glacial retreat).

facts.fact: L1 is unstable, as with L2.
About 1.5 million km sunward, uninterrupted Sun view, solar-storm warnings.
L1, L2 and L3 are unstable equilibrium points. Spacecraft need regular station-keeping. Only L4 and L5 are stable. Suggest “a point where gravity and orbital motion balance”.
About 1.5 million km from Earth on the far side from the Sun. Halo or Lissajous orbits.
ESA Venus orbiter with radar and spectrometers.

The £2.3 million grant and VenSpec-U detector testing are confirmed, but the team is Manish Patel’s Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group, not the CEI. The source says the OU is “participating in” science preparations, not heading them.
Dark-universe survey of billions of galaxies out to 10 billion light-years using weak lensing.
CEI characterised the CCD273 for VIS and runs trap-pumping analysis in the Euclid Science Ground Segment.

The CEI page says it developed the trap-pumping analysis routines, and the OU is credited with popularising the technique for space CCDs. “Developed and applied trap pumping for Euclid” is closer to the source.
Stephen Serjeant (OU) works on Euclid strong lensing and machine-learning lens finding (ELSA and OSCARS projects). Whether he leads a Euclid consortium group is not stated.
Subsurface ocean, young cracked ice shell, strong habitability candidate.
OU astrobiologists study ocean worlds with Arctic fieldwork on cryovolcanism and salts.

It reached Mars with the Trace Gas Orbiter but crashed on 19 October 2016 after a software error in the final descent.; ou_involvement: Manish Patel (OU) was a co-investigator on DREAMS, the lander’s environmental sensor package, which included the MicroARES electric-field sensor.
Launch 2028, lands at Oxia Planum, drill to 2 m.
landed_coords 18.1° N, 335.7° E (Oxia Planum).

facts.fact: ESA-led orbiter mapping trace gases like methane, and a relay for Curiosity and Perseverance.
An OU scientist is NOMAD Co-PI.
UVIS was designed at the OU. Further development, manufacture and assembly were done at Lambda-X in Belgium. Suggest “designed and led”.
UVIS data used for ozone, water vapour and trace gases, and to study water escape.
The OU supports CaSSIS operations and hosts one of the two CaSSIS Targeting Specialists; NOMAD and CaSSIS operations run from the OU's Interplanetary Space Operations Control area at Walton Hall.
Largest, most precise 3D map of the galaxy, nearly two billion stars.
CEI modelled charge trapping before launch, analysed the BP/RP and RVS radiation campaigns and fed the pipeline. Less in-flight damage than predicted, still being investigated.
Largest moon, bigger than Mercury, only moon with its own magnetic field, dark and grooved terrain.
Collected solar wind at L1 for over two years, hard landing in Utah (2004), measured the Sun’s O and N isotopes.

The key paper (McKeegan et al. 2011, Science) lists 13 authors from UCLA, LANL, Caltech, Montana, ASU, Bristol and Okayama, and none from the OU. The measurement used UCLA’s MegaSIMS. The finding (Sun enriched in ¹⁶O) is correct. Remove this unless the OU can point to its own Genesis paper.
Deployed rovers, kinetic impactor, returned Ryugu surface and subsurface samples. “En Route” fits its extended mission to 1998 KY26.
The OU oxygen isotope lab joined “Team Kochi”, one of three Japanese-led initial analysis teams.
ESA planetary defence mission launched 2024 to Didymos and Dimorphos, following up NASA’s DART impact. Arrives late 2026.
OU is involved in the Hera science team.
Launched 7 October 2024 (Falcon 9); Mars swingby 12 March 2025 at about 5,000 km altitude, also imaging Deimos.

ESA trajectory design: impulsive rendezvous with Didymos on 12 October 2026, then a two-month rendezvous phase of braking manoeuvres; DSM-2 in February 2026. Hera needs a wider orbit (farther aphelion) than Didymos to phase with it.

OU sub-millimetre research on distant galaxies.
Launched 1990, three decades of observations, contributed to the age of the universe and the discovery of dark energy.
WFC3’s CCDs are built by Teledyne e2v, which partners closely with the OU’s Centre for Electronic Imaging.
ESA probe, the only landing in the outer Solar System, 2005, a descent of about 2.5 hours, pebbles shaped by liquid methane.

NASA flagship to image Earth-like exoplanets with a coronagraph and search for biosignatures.

Innermost Galilean moon, most volcanically active body, tidal heating, sulfur colouring.
Modular microgravity laboratory. Partners are the US, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. First module launched 1998.
BIOMEX was led by DLR (PI Jean-Pierre de Vera). The OU was a participant: Karen Olsson-Francis (OU) is a co-author of the mission paper. Suggest “OU scientists took part in BIOMEX”.

Samples returned with Tim Peake in June 2016.
ESA mission launched 2023, arrives 2031, studies Ganymede, Europa and Callisto.
CEI and Teledyne e2v developed and characterised the CIS115 CMOS sensor for JANUS, including radiation testing.
JANUS was built under Italian leadership with contributions from the UK (Centre for Electronic Imaging, Open University), Spain and Germany; the OU is the UK institute on the team.
Waypoints: launch 14 April 2023, lunar–Earth flyby 20 August 2024, Venus 31 August 2025, Earth 28 September 2026, Earth January 2029, Jupiter July 2031.
The final Earth flyby is on 17 January 2029, putting JUICE on course for Jupiter in July 2031.
Largest planet, Great Red Spot, faint rings, strong gravity and magnetic field.
95 officially recognised. “About a hundred” is closer.
Launched 2021. Gold-coated mirror, infrared view of the first galaxies, exoplanet atmospheres.
OU researchers contributed to the WASP-39b studies.
The L 98-59 d paper acknowledges an OU-funded PhD studentship. No OU author found on the WASP-107b papers. Check before naming WASP-107b.
ESA electric-propulsion tug to Mars that then forms part of MARCONI.
The OU ARES group leads design of the High-Resolution Imager for Mars Exploration (HiRIME).

ISRO–JAXA mission: JAXA rover and ISRO lander, targeted for 2028 on H3.
The OU develops the Exploration Mass Spectrometer (EMS-L) for the LUPEX rover.
Heritage from flight hardware on Rosetta (Ptolemy) and Beagle 2 (GAP).
Iron oxide colouring, largest volcano and deepest canyons, thin atmosphere, polar caps, once warmer and wetter.
Long history: lander instruments (Beagle 2 GAP) and orbital atmospheric data (NOMAD UVIS).

Carried Beagle 2. An OU scientist is a co-investigator on its orbiter instruments. type: mission; parent: Mars; status: Operational; launch_year: 2003; description: ESA’s first Mars mission, in orbit since December 2003. Confirmed to the end of 2026, with an extension to 2028 to support JAXA’s MMX.; ou_involvement: Mars Express carried the OU-led Beagle 2 lander. John Murray (OU) was a co-investigator on the orbiter’s instrument teams (HRSC camera), per ESA’s payload documentation.
Planetary simulation yard on the Milton Keynes campus, used for rover driving in teaching.
Smallest planet, closest to the Sun, heavily cratered, geologically quiet, high density and a large metallic core.
The field is weak, about 1% of Earth’s. What surprised scientists is that it exists at all. Suggest “a magnetic field, which is surprising for such a small planet”.
OU scientists have studied Mercury’s surface composition and volcanic history for decades.
Only natural satellite, drives tides, stabilises Earth’s axis, regolith and mare basalts, only other body humans have visited.

The OU does lead ProSPA (ESA PROSPECT) and built the PITMS and EMS-L mass spectrometers, so the instrument part is right. “Leads international efforts in lunar research” is too broad for a source to support. Suggest naming ProSPA.
Car-sized rover in Gale Crater since 2012. Evidence of ancient lakes and organic molecules.
landed_coords −4.6°, 137.4° E.

Susanne Schwenzer is an MSL science team member as a collaborator of participating scientist John Bridges (Leicester). Her research is noble gases and water–rock interaction, as the file says. Suggest “science team members”.
Rescoped in 2023 as NewAthena. Adoption expected in Q1 2027, launch about 2037.
The shielding, GEANT4 and validation work is confirmed. The CEI page says it works “closely with institutions around the world” and does not say it leads.
Sub-orbital sounding rocket for high-resolution X-ray spectra (target Capella), a few minutes above the atmosphere.
The CEI page says XCAM designs and builds the camera. The CEI characterises and optimises the four CCD207-40 EMCCDs and programs the four BeagleBone Black computers.

That is State College, Pennsylvania (Penn State, the PI institution), not a launch site. Black Brant IX flights launch from Wallops (37.9° N, −75.5°) or White Sands (32.4° N, −106.3°). OGRE-P is slated for early 2027. Confirm the site with Penn State.
PIRATE and COAST robotic telescopes at Teide Observatory, operated remotely for teaching and research, including transits.
PIRATE began earlier (about 2008) and COAST earlier still. Check which date is meant.
Returned Bennu samples in September 2023. Now OSIRIS-APEX, bound for Apophis in 2029.
OU produced temperature predictions for the Nightingale site.
OU academics analyse returned Bennu material.
Astrobotic lander, propellant leak after launch in January 2024, payloads operated, re-entered.
It was the first US commercial lander attempt. Suggest “the first US commercial lunar lander to launch”.
The OU with RAL Space built the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer (PITMS) under ESA contract. It demonstrated full functionality in space.
Exploring Jezero for ancient life, caching samples, carried Ingenuity (first powered flight on another planet).
landed_coords 18.4° N, 77.5° E.
An OU researcher is on the NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return Campaign Science Group.
First landing on a comet nucleus in 2014, ten instruments, bounced, then hibernated.

The final Abydos site is about 8.15° S, 358.45° E (−1.55°) in the standard Cheops frame. The first touchdown (Agilkia) was 12.0° N, 335.7° E. The app’s value may be tuned to the 67P model’s own orientation, so check against the model before changing it.
Built jointly by RAL Space and the OU. Ptolemy’s results (Wright et al. 2015, Science) came alongside COSAC’s. “First chemical analysis of organics on a comet’s surface” is shared with COSAC.
Mapped the cosmic microwave background from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, refined age, composition and expansion.
26 cameras monitoring hundreds of thousands of bright stars for transits of Earth-sized planets.
Now March 2027 on Ariane 6.
OU population studies of astrophysical false positives (blended eclipsing binaries), funded by UKSA for the Development Phase.
CEI radiation-damage studies of PLATO’s CCDs.
Luna 27 is a Russian robotic south-polar lander with a drill for volatiles.

After 2022 ESA ended its Luna cooperation with Russia. PROSPECT (including the OU-led ProSPA) now flies on NASA CLPS CP-22, the Intuitive Machines IM-4 Nova-C lander, launching 2027 to about 84.5° S, 31.5° E. Consider renaming or replacing this entry (see the Missing missions tab).
The OU leads development of ProSPA, which heats drilled samples and analyses them by mass spectrometry.

The home of the OU-led ProSPA now that it no longer flies on Luna 27. Field of view 100 times Hubble’s at similar resolution, dark energy and exoplanet surveys, technology-demonstration coronagraph.
CEI worked under contract to JPL from 2014 to 2019 on the coronagraph EMCCD, resulting in the CCD311, a customised CCD201 selected for flight.
Launched 30 August 2026 on Falcon Heavy. Should be “Launched” or “En Route”, 2026.
First long-term study of a comet nucleus, orbited 67P for over two years.
OU co-developed Ptolemy with RAL Space.
OU contributed to MUPUS and GIADA.
OU coordinated the international ground-based observing campaign.
Ryugu is an Apollo asteroid whose orbit crosses Earth’s (0.96–1.41 AU). The rest (dark, diamond-shaped, rubble pile, boulders) is correct.
Rings of ice and rock, second largest planet, low density (would float).
The NASA fact sheet lists 274. “Hundreds of moons” is now correct.
The NASA fact sheet gives 0.052 (mean) and JPL’s J2000 elements give 0.054. 0.057 is high. Visually minor.
OU Cassini dust work exists (Cosmic Dust Analyser papers by Green, McBride and Hillier). Enceladus modelling and weather work not found.
Three now: Sentinel-2C launched 5 September 2024, and 2A continues in an extended campaign alongside 2B and 2C.
High-resolution optical imaging for Copernicus: vegetation, soil, water, frequent revisits.
Ocean and land monitoring: sea-surface topography, temperature and colour.
This technique exists (for example ESA’s SEN-ET project and Guzinski & Nieto 2019), but those papers are by DHI and others, not the OU. Ask for the OU publication.
Launched 19 May 2026 on Vega-C. The 9 April date was postponed.
ESA–CAS mission for the first global X-ray images of the magnetosphere and its interaction with the solar wind.
Twin CCD370s, 4510 × 4510 pixels of 18 µm, form the SXI focal plane. The CEI tested noise, CTI and defects before flight.
PLATO has not flown (launch now March 2027). The CCD370 derives from the CCD270 developed for PLATO. Suggest “developed for PLATO”.
The OU says the CEI has spent over a decade “developing and testing” them. Teledyne e2v manufactures them. “Developed and characterised” is safer than “designed”.

Planet semi-major axes (J2000, AU): Mercury 0.38709927, Venus 0.72333566, Earth-Moon barycentre 1.00000261, Mars 1.52371034, Jupiter 5.20288700, Saturn 9.53667594, Uranus 19.18916464, Neptune 30.06992276.
NASA Great Observatory, TRAPPIST-1 planets, over 16 years of operations (2003–2020).
First return of comet coma and interstellar dust, captured in aerogel. Capsule landed 2006.
OU researchers used IR, UV/visible and Raman spectroscopy on Wild 2 grains in preliminary examination.
Yellow dwarf at the centre of the Solar System, holds it together by gravity, more than 99% of its mass.
Gamma-ray burst observatory that slews to afterglows, operating for over 20 years.

Swift has not been decommissioned. A commercial reboost failed in August 2026, and it resumed UVOT and XRT science. NASA expects re-entry around the end of 2026. Use “Operational” for now, then “Re-entered”.
Largest moon of Saturn, thick atmosphere, methane and ethane lakes, methane cycle, dunes and mountains.
The Nature Astronomy map (2019) was led by Rosaly Lopes at JPL. None of its 13 authors is at the OU. The OU web article about it is a commentary by David Rothery. Six terrain types is correct.
The first global geomorphological map of Titan (Lopes et al. 2019, Nature Astronomy) was led by JPL; none of its 13 authors is at the OU.
UK-led, delivered by ESA, a “gold standard” climate calibration mission measuring incoming and reflected radiation.
CEI radiation-damage study of the Teledyne e2v CIS120: dark current, noise and QE before and after gamma and proton irradiation at several temperatures.
First UK Space Agency mission, a CubeSat technology demonstrator. Completed after about 14 months of operations.
Payloads for space weather and secure communications.

CEI won one of three science payload slots for C3D. Launched July 2014, three cameras, first in-orbit test of a European 0.18 µm CMOS imager. Dark-current and flatband shifts like CCDs, plus single-event upsets.
29 as of 2025. S/2025 U1 was found by JWST and announced in August 2025, following a 28th in 2023.
Ice giant on its side, methane gives the blue-green colour, faint rings.
Earth’s twin in size, thick CO₂ atmosphere and runaway greenhouse, retrograde rotation, surface hot enough to melt lead, sulfuric acid clouds.

Listed as a current CEI mission. type: mission; parent: Earth; status: Planned; launch_year: 2031 or later (repeatedly delayed); description: A Russian-led ultraviolet space observatory for 115–310 nm, with Spain and Japan as partners.; ou_involvement: The Centre for Electronic Imaging studies radiation damage to the CCD camera’s sensors and their ability to integrate for long periods at very low noise.
